Reference · Curricular Analytics

Curricular Analytics

Framework, metrics, APIs, data pipeline, and PowerBI usage — compiled from the Curricular Analytics reference document.

What is Curricular Analytics

An open-source framework and methodology designed to visualize, quantify, and analyze the structural complexity of academic programs.

Instead of just looking at a degree as a checklist of classes, it treats a curriculum as a network (a directed acyclic graph) to understand how course requirements impact student progression and graduation rates.

How does it normally work: Upload

Uploading Curricula and Degree Plans - File Formats

In order to upload a curriculum or degree plan to the Curricular Analytics site, you simply need to specify them in a CSV file, and then upload them to your account as described above.

1. Definition & Scope

  • Curriculum: The foundational blueprint of an academic program. It is the absolute set of courses, credit hours (e.g., a minimum of 60 for an associate degree or 120 for a bachelor's), and specific learning outcomes a student must successfully complete to earn the degree.
  • Degree Plan: A structural roadmap or schedule. It is a term-by-term arrangement (semesters or quarters) that maps out exactly when a student will take those required courses, organized in a way that satisfies all prerequisite and co-requisite rules.

2. Relationship (One-to-Many)

  • There is a one-to-many relationship between a curriculum and its degree plans.
  • A single curriculum can have many different valid degree plans depending on a student's individual pacing, background, or needs.

Output

Curricula Metrics

Blocking Factor

The blocking factor is an important curriculum-based metric because it measures the extent to which one course blocks the ability to take other courses in the curriculum. That is, a course with a high blocking factor acts as a gateway to many other courses in the curriculum. Students who are unable to pass the gateway course will be blocked from taking many other courses in the curriculum.

The blocking factor of each course is shown inside of the course vertices in this figure.

Delay Factor

Many curricula, particularly those in science, technology engineering and math (STEM) fields, contain a set of courses that must be completed in sequential order. The ability to successfully navigate these long pathways without delay is critical for student success and on-time graduation. If any course on the pathway is not completed on time, the student will then be delayed in completing the entire pathway by one term. The delay factor metric allows us to quantify this effect.

. As an example of the delay factor metric, consider the same four-course curricula shown above. The delay factor of each course is shown inside of the course vertices in the figure below.

Centrality

A course can be thought of as being central to a curriculum if it requires a number of foundational courses as prerequisites, and the course itself serves as a prerequisite to many additional discipline-specific courses in the curriculum. The centrality metric is meant to capture this notion.

We define the centrality of source and sink vertices to be 0. For all other course vertices, consider all of the long paths (i.e., unique paths from a source to a sink) containing course vertex is given by the sum of these path lengths. As an example of the centrality metric, consider the same four-course curricula shown above. The centrality factor of each course is shown inside of the vertices in the figure below. In the case of the curriculum in part (a), there is one long path of length three that includes course hence its centrality is 3, while in part (b), there are two long paths of length three that include course, hence its centrality is 6.

Structural Complexity

The curricular complexity of a course is meant to capture the impact of curricular structure on student progression. Through experimentation, we have found that a simple linear combination of the delay and blocking factors described above provides a good measure for quantifying the structural complexity of a curriculum. Specifically, we have found a high correlation between increased structural complexity and decreased graduation rates.

As an example of the structural complexity metric, consider the same four-course curricula shown above. The complexity factor of each course, which is simply the sum of the course's delay and blocking factors, are shown inside of the course vertices in this figure.

How we process data

Available Data (dbCompass in sdw-d-db.aws.uci.edu)

[dbcompass].[CA].[TB_Actual_DegreePlan_ANON_CA_Metrics]

SQL

SELECT TOP (1000) [Student_ID_ANON]
,[Institution]
,[AcademicYear]
,[Curriculum]
,[DegreePlan]
,[DegreeType]
,[SystemType]
,[CIP]
,[CourseSequenceID]
,[CourseName]
,[Prefix]
,[Number]
,[Prerequisites]
,[Corequisites]
,[Strict_Corequisites]
,[CreditHours]
,[CanonicalName]
,[TermNumber]
,[Course_URL]
,[Plan_URL]
,[Notes]
,[ExtractDate]
,[DegreePlanID]
,[CA_Blocking_Factor]
,[CA_Delay_Factor]
,[CA_Centrality]
,[CA_Structural_Complexity]
,[CA_MetricDate]
,[DB_INSERT_TIMESTAMP]
FROM [dbcompass].[CA].[TB_Actual_DegreePlan_ANON_CA_Metrics]
WHERE Student_ID_ANON='S00530182'
order by [CourseSequenceID]
